chunks: "Both describe how the output stage of a pin is built. Push-pull means two transistors: a PMOS connecting the pin to VDD and an NMOS connecting it to ground.
To output a 1, the PMOS turns on, which pushes the pin up; to output a 0, the NMOS turns on, which pulls it down.
One of them is always on, so the pin is always actively driven and has a low impedance in both states.
Open-drain means there's only the NMOS, and its drain goes to the pin with nothing else attached inside the chip, that's the 'open' part.
To output a 0, the NMOS turns on and pulls the pin to ground. To output a 1, the NMOS turns off, and the pin is just released, floating.
It only goes high if something outside, a pull-up resistor to some voltage, pulls it up.

The practical consequences: with open-drain I need that external resistor, the high level is set by whatever voltage the resistor goes to, and several open-drain outputs can share one line because none of them ever fights.
That's the wired-AND used on I2C, interrupts and resets. Push-pull needs no resistor and is faster, but two of them can't safely share a line."
